evidenceAudit.scope: Adults with chronic heart failure (HFrEF, HFmrEF, HFpEF) in primary and specialist care: diagnosis with NT-proBNP and echocardiography, the four foundational medicines, titration and monitoring, devices and follow-up. Verified against the Saudi Heart Association HF guideline 2019 and its 2023 focused update (National Heart Center/SHA), and NICE NG106 (2025 update). Starting doses and contraindications from US FDA prescribing information. Acute decompensated heart failure is covered in the Acute Heart Failure topic.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 12 Oct 2026.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: Bisoprolol HF titration (not in FDA label) — local protocol
IV iron dosing — product SmPC/local protocol
SHA device recommendation tables not reproduced

pathophysiology.summary: Heart failure is a clinical syndrome of symptoms (breathlessness, fatigue, ankle swelling) caused by a structural or functional cardiac abnormality, with raised natriuretic peptides or objective congestion. It is classified by left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF): reduced (HFrEF, 40% or less), mildly reduced (HFmrEF, 41–49%) and preserved (HFpEF, 50% or more) (SHA 2023).
keyMechanisms: Myocardial injury (ischaemia, hypertension, cardiomyopathy, valve disease) lowers cardiac output → activation of the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system and sympathetic nervous system.
Neurohormonal activation causes sodium and water retention, vasoconstriction and adverse remodelling (dilatation, fibrosis) — the targets of ACE inhibitor/ARNI, beta-blocker and MRA therapy.
SGLT2 inhibitors reduce HF hospitalisation and cardiovascular death across the LVEF spectrum (SHA 2023).
Raised wall stress releases BNP/NT-proBNP; levels support diagnosis and prognosis but do not separate HF types (NICE).
HFpEF: stiff ventricle with impaired filling, usually with hypertension, obesity, diabetes, AF and older age.

symptoms: Breathlessness on exertion, orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea.
Ankle or leg swelling; weight gain; abdominal bloating.
physicalSigns: Raised jugular venous pressure, displaced apex beat, third heart sound.
Bibasal crackles, pleural effusion; peripheral oedema; hepatomegaly.
NYHA class I–IV for symptom severity.
redFlags: Breathlessness at rest, hypoxia, hypotension or cold peripheries — acute decompensation
Potassium above 5.5 mmol/L or creatinine rise above 50% on RAAS inhibitors/MRA
Heart rate below 50/min or second/third-degree heart block on beta-blocker

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Normal echo and natriuretic peptide (obesity lowers NT-proBNP).
Blood tests; can cause or worsen HF.

differentials.condition: Nephrotic syndrome, liver disease, venous insufficiency

ruleIn.expectedFinding: Above 2,000 ng/L: specialist assessment and echo within 2 weeks; 400–2,000 ng/L: within 6 weeks.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Below 400 ng/L in an untreated person makes HF less likely (NICE). Obesity, diuretics and ACE inhibitors/ARNI/ARB lower levels; AF, CKD and age raise them.
ruleIn.normalValue: NT-proBNP below 400 ng/L (NICE threshold for referral)

clinicalManagement.title: Confirm and classify
actions: History, examination, ECG and NT-proBNP; refer for echocardiography by NT-proBNP band (NICE).
Classify by LVEF: HFrEF 40% or less, HFmrEF 41–49%, HFpEF 50% or more (SHA 2023).
Look for the cause: ischaemia, hypertension, valve disease, arrhythmia, cardiomyopathy, alcohol.

clinicalManagement.title: HFrEF — four foundational medicines
actions: Give all four: ACE inhibitor (or ARNI), beta-blocker, MRA and SGLT2 inhibitor unless contraindicated (SHA 2023, NICE 2025).
It is not necessary to reach the target dose of one medicine before starting the next (NICE).
Switch ACE inhibitor to sacubitril/valsartan if still symptomatic on maximum tolerated doses; stop the ACE inhibitor 36 h before (NICE, label).
ACE-inhibitor intolerance (not angioedema): ARNI; after angioedema: beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor and consider an ARB (NICE).

SHA target doses: enalapril 20 mg twice daily, lisinopril 20–40 mg daily, ramipril 10 mg daily, bisoprolol 10 mg daily, carvedilol 25 mg twice daily, metoprolol succinate 200 mg daily, candesartan 32 mg daily, valsartan 160 mg twice daily, sacubitril/valsartan 97/103 mg twice daily, spironolactone or eplerenone 50 mg daily, ivabradine 7.5 mg twice daily.

branches.condition: Still symptomatic, sinus rhythm 75/min or more
actions: Ivabradine (specialist).

branches.condition: ACE inhibitor, ARNI and ARB all not tolerated
actions: Specialist advice; consider hydralazine with a nitrate (NICE).

branches.condition: Worsening or severe HFrEF despite optimised therapy
actions: Digoxin with specialist advice (NICE).

clinicalManagement.title: Congestion
actions: Loop diuretic at the lowest dose that keeps the patient euvolaemic; titrate up and down (NICE). SHA usual furosemide range 40–240 mg/day.
Daily weights; flexible diuretic plan for patients who can self-manage.

clinicalManagement.title: HFmrEF and HFpEF
actions: SGLT2 inhibitor for all with HFmrEF and HFpEF (SHA 2023); NICE: consider an MRA and SGLT2 inhibitor in HFpEF.
HFmrEF: consider ACE inhibitor, beta-blocker and MRA as well (NICE; SHA: may be considered).
Diuretics for congestion; treat hypertension, AF, diabetes, obesity.

clinicalManagement.title: Other measures
actions: IV iron if iron deficient (see investigations).
Avoid verapamil, diltiazem and short-acting dihydropyridines in HFrEF (NICE); avoid NSAIDs and thiazolidinediones.
Devices: ICD and cardiac resynchronisation therapy per SHA 2019 Tables 13–14 — refer to cardiology.
Annual influenza and one-off pneumococcal vaccination (NICE). Anticoagulate if AF (per AF guideline).
Pregnancy: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, ARNI, MRAs, ivabradine, vericiguat and SGLT2 inhibitors are contraindicated — stop before conception (SHA 2023).

clinicalManagement.title: Monitoring
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Every 2 weeks while titrating; at least 6-monthly when stable
actions: Functional capacity, fluid status, rhythm, cognition, nutrition and medicines review (NICE).
Renal function and potassium 1–2 weeks after each change; BP before and after each increment; heart rate and ECG with beta-blocker titration.

learningObjectives: Diagnose, classify and manage chronic heart failure with guideline-directed medicines, titration and monitoring.

keyPoints: NT-proBNP first; echo to classify by LVEF.
HFrEF: four pillars — ACEi/ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor.
Start low, go slow, but start all four early.
Check potassium and creatinine 1–2 weeks after each change.
SGLT2 inhibitors help every LVEF category.
pitfalls: Waiting to reach target dose of one drug before starting the next.
Stopping RAAS blockers for a modest creatinine rise.
Starting ARNI within 36 h of an ACE inhibitor.
Non-dihydropyridine CCBs or NSAIDs in HFrEF.
Low NT-proBNP in obesity falsely reassuring.

patientEducation: Daily weights; act on gain of 2 kg in 3 days per local plan.
Medicine purpose, side effects and sick-day rules.
Symptoms of worsening HF and when to seek help.
lifestyleAndDiet: Regular exercise as tolerated; cardiac rehabilitation.
Moderate salt intake; avoid excess fluid if hyponatraemic or congested (individualise).
dischargeCriteria: Euvolaemic on a stable diuretic dose.
Foundational medicines started with a titration plan.
Bloods booked 1–2 weeks after changes; HF nurse/clinic follow-up arranged.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review every 2 weeks during titration; stable patients at least every 6 months with renal function and potassium every 3–6 months (NICE). Specialist HF team and cardiac rehabilitation; palliative care when appropriate.
